newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU curbs wheat exports as drought menaces crops. [CORRECTED 14:50 GMT]
newsitem.headline: EU curbs wheat exports as drought menaces crops. [CORRECTED 14:50 GMT]

text.p: The European Union has reimposed a tax on wheat exports to stop scarce supplies escaping abroad and to dampen internal prices inflamed by prolonged dry weather and risk of crop damage.

The move, announced on Thursday, closed the last channel for EU wheat exports this season and follows a surge in world prices above EU levels on fears that drought in Europe and frost in the United States will blight 1997 grain harvests.

"The export levy...is due to uncertainty about the impact of weather on cereals production in the next EU harvest and also on the world market," European Commission agriculture spokesman Gerard Kiely told a news briefing.
The EU action is likely to irritate the United States which attacked a similar tax at the start of the marketing year last July saying taxes, like subsidies, distorted trade.
But EU officials said the tax conformed with open trading rules managed by the World Trade Organisation.
The EU move came despite a record EU cereals harvest of just over 200 million tonnes last year and early indications of another massive crop in 1997 following an easing of planting restrictions.

But EU public grain stocks have slumped to just over one million tonnes from 2.6 million tonnes at the start of the season last July, and from a peak of 33 million tonnes before cost-cutting reforms were implemented in 1993.
Kiely said the levy was imposed because the market was over-heating due to internal and external climatic influences.
EU prices have risen substantially and in some regions were more than 20 percent above the intervention level, he noted.
"The export levy is aimed at dampening prices on the EU market and to ensure sufficient control on exports to avoid any shortages developing," Kiely said.
Kiely added that one of the objectives of the EU's Common Agricultural Policy is to stabilise prices.

For much of the past 40 years, the EU has been preoccupied with preventing prices falling too far but it must also avoid prices climbing too high and harming the interests of flour millers and the animal feed industry.
"We will have no hesitation in changing that levy if it needs to be increased or reduced in the light of market developments," Kiely said.
EU grain sources said that the European Commission was only applying agreed criteria for introducing an export levy.
"It's the force of circumstances," said one source adding that the EU was not responsible for either drought or frost.
World wheat prices were seen nearing EU levels and could overtake them this summer with the risk that EU grain would be sucked abroad, tightening domestic supplies and squeezing prices upwards.
(Corrects to make clear that although world wheat prices are close to EU levels, they have not yet overtaken them).
"There's a risk of market disruption," another source said.
Trade sources noted an increasing risk of volatile grain markets because none of the major producers was now prepared to continue the expense of holding large stocks."
"In future every climatic incident will provoke a violent market reaction," one trade source predicted.
